extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, criminology, political economy, and activists interested in race/class analyses of crime and policing
extracted.subtask_short: analysing crime within Marxist class theory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical, historically grounded analysis of how 'crime', the lumpenproletariat, domestic/wageless labour, and policing relate to capitalist production and class struggle. The text evaluates competing Marxist and radical-feminist positions about political significance and strategic role of various marginal strata (criminal poor, black wageless, housewives) under modern capitalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the criminal underworld to social and labour movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The underworld (as distinct from, say, peasant bandits) rarely take part in wider social and revolutionary movements ... on the whole this type of criminality has only marginal interest for the historian of social and labour movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether criminal activity is integrated with broader social/labour movements (organic) or remains parasitic/marginal (conjunctural). Note exceptions/overlaps in slum quarters, semi-proletarian concentrations and minority ghettoes where substitution or idealisation may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of criminal classes to play a fundamental revolutionary role
rubrics_metrics.description: Three propositions: criminal social movements cannot play a fundamental role because (1) their position is marginal to productive life and social formations; (2) historically they have become marginal to the proletariat which replaced them at the centre of political struggle; (3) the form of consciousness traditionally developed by this stratum is not adequate to that required by a class which aims to supplant one mode of production by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to judge claims that criminal groups can be decisive political agents. Check empirical placement of the group in production relations and evaluate the form and organization of their collective consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marxist account of crime as 'unproductive' or redistributive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime (theft) is merely redistributive; like prostitution, gambling or racketeering, it is a form of 'unproductive' rather than 'productive' labour and though it may be 'illegal' with respect to norms governing normal capitalist relations, it is most often 'capitalistic' in form (e.g. organised criminal enterprises) — i.e. adapted to the system on which it is parasitic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate criminal phenomena in light of their relation to production: are they redistributive/unproductive, or do they have forms that reproduce or parasitically integrate with capitalist forms (organized crime)? Distinguish moral/ethical critique from materialist analysis of production relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical specificity and definition of the lumpenproletariat
rubrics_metrics.description: How historically specific was Marx's analysis of the composition and nature of the lumpenproletariat? The question of whether contemporary groups correspond to Marx's 'lumpen' requires serious theoretical and definitional work rather than simple empirical labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the 'lumpenproletariat' label, compare to Marx/Engels' historical list (vagabonds, discharged soldiers, jailbirds, swindlers, ragpickers, etc.) and assess whether analogous strata exist under monopoly/modern capitalism; avoid anachronistic or careless identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'productive' and 'unproductive' labour and the role of reproduction spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Marx's distinction: productive labour directly produces surplus value; unproductive labour does not, but spheres of reproduction (family, state, circulation) are necessary to capital's circuit. Unproductive sectors have expanded in modern capitalism and perform key functions for capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss unproductive labour as irrelevant — analyze how domestic, service, and state-paid labour contribute to the reproduction and realisation of capital. Use Volume II/III insights: reproduction of labour-power is essential and exploited by capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating domestic labour (housework) as productive or politically strategic
rubrics_metrics.description: Housework may be 'unproductive' strictly speaking, but it contributes to the production of the commodity 'labour-power' and participates in social production. 'Wages for housework' frames refusal to perform domestic labour as a lever of social power against capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether analyses treat housework as merely marginal or as central to reproduction of labour-power; consider feminist arguments (Selma James, Power of Women) that domestic labour can be mobilized strategically (refusal to work) and is exploited by capital (double exploitation via sexual division of labour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic role of 'wagelessness' and refusal to work in class struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Race Today: high levels of youthful black unemployment are interpreted as a conscious political 'refusal to work' that subverts capital by refusing to act as a reserve army and thereby undermines capital's ability to maximize surplus-value from immigrant/workless labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that 'wagelessness' is a form of political struggle: examine whether refusal to work is organized/autonomous and whether it materially interrupts capital's mechanisms (labour supply, wage discipline). Consider policing as an attempt to reintegrate the wageless into wage-labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomous sectoral struggle and the 'hierarchy of labour-powers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Selma James: the international division of labour accentuates a 'hierarchy of labour-powers' splitting the working class along racial, sexual, national and generational lines; each sector must make its autonomous power felt and by specificity of experience redefine class and class struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge movements by whether they assert autonomous sectoral struggle and whether such struggles can be strategic levers for broader class transformation. Beware reductionist views that deny the political potential of identity-based or sectoral movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of the recomposition of capital and the 'mass worker' (social-capital thesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary Italian-Marxist variant: present phase characterized as 'social capital' (subsummation of many capitals into one, socialisation of accumulation), with Fordist reorganisation of labour, Keynesian management and social-democratic integration producing a massified, deskilled 'mass worker' and new forms of political recomposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about working-class recomposition, examine structural changes (Fordist production, Keynesianism, integration of labour institutions), the emergence of massified labour, and how these shifts alter the strategic placement of different strata (including black labour) in struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of refusal to work as ideological versus political (Black Liberator critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Black Liberator collective argues the refusal to work among black youth is an ideological phenomenon, not a political struggle that 'subverts capital' directly; black workers are better conceptualized as a racially differentiated 'reserve army of labour' and as super-exploited when productively employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether evidence supports Race Today's political reading of wagelessness or the Black Liberator's more classical labour-market/reserve-army interpretation; consider implications for policing explanations — whether police aim to regulate class struggle or are operating at a different level of state-economic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex relation between economic class position and political agency/form
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship between classes constituted in the economic relations of capitalist production and the forms in which they appear as political forces is no simple matter — variations in production forms, social reproduction, state formation, and historical contexts produce infinite gradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In any evaluative or theoretical account, link economic-base positions (production/reproduction roles, reserve army dynamics) to political appearances and agency carefully; avoid simplistic causal reductions of political forms to economic base without attending to institutional, racial, gendered, and historical mediations.
